analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to block big mergers, penalizes dominant companies that crush competition, and rewards antitrust whistleblowers.
analysis.headline: The antitrust overhaul, backed by 11 of 48 Senate Democrats, never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the nation's antitrust laws to make it easier for the government to stop big mergers, crack down on dominant companies that squeeze out competitors, and impose stiff penalties on lawbreaking firms. It would also fund the antitrust agencies, protect workers who report price-fixing, and stop companies from forcing antitrust disputes into private arbitration. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, small businesses, and workers would benefit from tougher antitrust enforcement: the bill targets higher prices, lower quality, and reduced choice caused by market power, explicitly recognizes that dominant employers can push down wages, creates new tools to challenge mergers and exclusionary conduct, funds the antitrust agencies, protects and rewards whistleblowers, and blocks companies from forcing antitrust claims into private arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lowers the legal bar for stopping harmful mergers, replacing the current 'substantially to lessen competition' standard with 'an appreciable risk of materially lessening competition,' and spells out that harm to quality, choice, innovation, workers, and suppliers counts, not just price.

It creates bright-line rules that shift the burden of proof to merging companies: a merger over $5 billion, or an acquisition of a $50 million-plus company by a firm valued at more than $100 billion, is presumed anticompetitive unless the companies prove otherwise.

It makes it unlawful for dominant firms (generally those with more than 50% market share) to engage in exclusionary conduct that risks harming competition, with civil penalties up to 15% of the firm's total U.S. revenue or 30% of revenue in the affected market.
It adds major new civil penalties for Sherman Act price-fixing and monopolization violations, using the same revenue-based formula, on top of existing criminal and private remedies.

It protects employees, contractors, and agents from retaliation for reporting antitrust violations, and lets whistleblowers earn 10% to 30% of criminal fines their information helps the government collect.
It bans predispute forced arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for antitrust disputes, so consumers and small businesses can band together in court.
It funds enforcement with $535 million for the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and $725 million for the FTC in fiscal 2025, plus dedicated merger filing fees afterward.
It recognizes in the bill's findings that dominant employers use market power to hold down wages, and explicitly extends merger scrutiny to monopsony power over workers and suppliers.

analysis.who_pays: Dominant firms would pay: civil penalties of up to 15% of their U.S. revenue (or 30% in the affected market) for exclusionary conduct or antitrust violations, heavier scrutiny and a reversed burden of proof for large mergers, mandatory annual reporting on consummated mergers, and higher merger filing fees to fund enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The presumption rules could block or deter mergers that would actually benefit consumers, since companies over $100 billion in market cap or a deal over $5 billion would bear the burden of proving a deal harmless even when it is.

The revenue-based penalties are large enough to impose real compliance and litigation costs across the economy, and businesses argue broadened liability risks chilling ordinary competitive behavior like aggressive discounting or product design, though the bill exempts good-faith patent enforcement and legally required conduct.
The bill drew no Republican support, so opponents' core objection is that it would hand executive-branch agencies broad discretion over mergers and market conduct with less judicial checking.
Its funding relies on merger filing fees, which concentrate new costs on the dealmaking industry and are tied to merger activity levels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains are large but diffuse: stronger competition historically shows up as lower prices, higher wages, and more small-business opportunities across the whole economy, while the costs — penalties, deal uncertainty, and compliance — fall on a concentrated set of very large firms. The main honest objection is design risk: bright-line presumptions for large mergers and 15%-of-revenue penalties are blunt instruments that could catch some procompetitive deals and conduct, and the bill's complete lack of Republican support suggests real disagreement about how much discretion to hand enforcement agencies. On balance, the bill's costs fall mainly on the companies with the most market power, which is the point.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 9, 2024, with 11 Democratic cosponsors as original supporters.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, its only action of the Congress.
The bill received no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no House counterpart action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
No Senate Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving its support confined to a minority of the Democratic caucus.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies that would have faced the bill's new merger presumptions and revenue-based civil penalties are better off because it died; they continue to operate under the current, lighter antitrust rules. Consumers, workers, and small businesses gain nothing from the bill's failure except the avoidance of its compliance costs, which its supporters considered small next to the cost of concentrated market power.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Competition and Antitrust Law Enforcement Reform Act of 2024.

for.name: 11 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed before the Congress ended.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, and the committee controlled by the party caucus with the majority (Democrats held 48 of 100 seats through organizing agreements) took no action on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 original supporters were Democrats, all 11 cosponsors were Senate Democrats, and no Republican signed on before the bill died in committee.

industries.industry: Dominant national corporations (large tech platforms, big-box retail, and other firms with 50%+ market share)
industries.note: The bill directly targets firms with over 50% market share or more than $100 billion in market cap, exposing them to revenue-based civil penalties and presumptively unlawful mergers. Their business models built on dominant market positions would face far higher legal risk.

industries.industry: Mega-merger dealmaking (investment banks, private equity, and merger advisors)
industries.note: Deals over $5 billion, or any acquisition of a $50 million-plus company by a $100 billion-plus firm, would be presumed anticompetitive unless the parties prove otherwise. This raises the cost and risk of large-scale dealmaking and private-equity rollups.

industries.industry: Antitrust defense bar and compliance firms
industries.note: The bill would add new civil penalty regimes, reporting requirements, and enforcement guidelines, expanding demand for antitrust litigation and compliance counsel. Its interest runs with stricter enforcement even as clients pay for it.
